paragraphs: Sometimes the market price of a product rises because of rules made by the government. Such a higher price can last as long as the rules that cause it.

The market price of a product may stay above its natural price for a long time. But it can rarely stay below it for long. If any part of the price is paid below the natural rate, the people affected will feel the loss at once. They will quickly stop using so much land, labour or capital to make that product. As a result, the amount brought to market will soon be just enough to meet the real demand. This means the demand of people who can pay. So the market price will soon rise again to the natural price. This, at least, is what happens where there is perfect freedom.

In fact, the same laws about apprentices and trade groups can work in two directions. When an industry is doing well, they allow the worker to raise his wages well above their natural rate. When the industry declines, they sometimes force him to accept wages well below it. In the first case they keep many people out of his job. In the second case they keep him out of many other jobs.

However, these rules do not lower wages for as long as they raise them. They can keep wages high for many centuries. But they can keep them low only during the lives of certain workers. These are the workers who learned the trade when it was doing well. When those workers are gone, the number of people trained in the trade will naturally adjust to the real demand. Only a very harsh system can push wages or profits below their natural rate in a particular job for several generations. Such a system existed in Indostan and in ancient Egypt. There, religion forced every man to follow his father's job. Changing it was seen as a terrible crime against religion.
This is all I need to say for now about market prices that move away from natural prices. Sometimes this happens for a short time, and sometimes for good.

The natural price itself changes with the natural rate of each of its parts: wages, profit and rent. In every society this rate depends on the situation of that society. Is it rich or poor? Is it growing, standing still or declining? In the next four chapters, I will try to explain the causes of these changes as fully and clearly as I can.

First, I will try to explain which conditions naturally decide the rate of wages. I will also explain how these conditions are affected when a society is rich or poor, growing, standing still or declining.
Second, I will try to show which conditions naturally decide the rate of profit. I will also show how the same changes in the society affect these conditions.
